text: A Windows login password protects a machine while it's running and someone is trying to sign in normally — it does nothing if someone just pulls the drive out and reads it on another computer entirely. This lesson covers BitLocker's full-disk encryption, the TPM chip that protects its key, and the recovery key you need when the TPM won't release that key through the normal path.

Without BitLocker, a stolen laptop's drive can be pulled and mounted on another machine, and every file on it is just sitting there, fully readable — the login screen never even got a chance to run. With BitLocker enabled, that same removed drive is encrypted end to end: the operating system, every application, every user file, and even free space, not just a folder someone remembered to protect.

BitLocker's key lives in the TPM, a dedicated security chip on the motherboard, kept separate from the drive itself. Before releasing that key, the TPM validates the boot process — checking that the boot loader and early startup components haven't been tampered with. If that check fails, the TPM withholds the key, and the drive stays encrypted and unreadable even though it's physically intact.

Because a firmware update, a motherboard change, or a forgotten PIN can all make the TPM legitimately withhold its key, BitLocker generates a 48-digit numerical recovery key the moment encryption is turned on — meant to be stored somewhere other than the encrypted drive itself, whether printed, saved to a USB drive, or backed up automatically to Active Directory or Microsoft Entra ID for domain-joined machines.

BitLocker protects confidentiality the moment a device leaves the building, turning a stolen laptop into a stolen piece of hardware instead of a confirmed data breach. Next: Chapter 3 shifts from hardening the machine to watching it — starting with Windows Event Viewer and the Security Log, where every one of these settings leaves a trace.
